Clashes Erupt in French Cities After Largely Peaceful Cost-of-Living Protests

Protests in France draw hundreds of thousands amid evening clashes

Tens of thousands of people marched across France on Saturday in a third wave of demonstrations over the cost of living and deteriorating public services, according to the interior ministry. The rallies included participants in Halloween fancy dress and passed off largely peacefully during the day, though clashes erupted in Paris, Lyon, Toulouse and other cities as evening fell.

Confirmed figures and official statements

The interior ministry said about 320,000 people took part in rallies nationwide, down from an estimated 410,000 the previous weekend. Around 70,000 marched in Paris along boulevards on the south-eastern outskirts, avoiding the city centre. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said roughly 150 planned demonstrations had proceeded peacefully, but that police faced an “extraordinary” level of violence from some rioters as the rallies ended.

The ministry reported 565 arrests across the country. In Paris, four police officers and one gendarme were injured. Nuñez said one riot police officer in Paris had been hit by a Molotov cocktail, which he described as an attempted murder.

Where clashes occurred

  • Paris: Dozens of masked people dressed in black used hammers to pry up paving stones and hurl them at police near the Porte de Charenton, according to the Paris police prefecture. At least one incendiary device was thrown at security forces. Police responded with teargas and baton charges. The prefecture described a “hardcore of several hundred rioters” attacking officers with projectiles.
  • Lyon: Protesters threw projectiles at police, prompting officers to fire teargas.
  • Toulouse: Police used water cannon against an unauthorised protest that drew several thousand people, mostly young demonstrators.

Who took part

The marches brought together school students, trade unions and gilets jaunes (yellow vests) protesters. Participants cited anger at the cost of living, widening inequalities and the government of President Emmanuel Macron.

One protester on the Paris march, Jérôme Rodrigues, said the French economy was being run by “a group of incompetents” while families struggled. Camille Guérin, a protester in Nantes, said demonstrators were rejecting the cost of living and the far right while supporting high school students’ demands.

Sabrine Kharbach of the student organisation Union Étudiante said students would stage new high school and university blockades on Tuesday and Thursday, then join a 5 November demonstration called by workers and trade unions.

Broader European context

Protests also occurred in Germany, where police used water cannon and teargas to disperse crowds in cities including Frankfurt, Cologne and Berlin. In Frankfurt, at least two stores were looted as protests turned violent, according to a Reuters witness. In Albania’s capital, Tirana, protesters renewed demands that Prime Minister Edi Rama resign; masked youths threw paving stones and firebombs at police after a peaceful start outside the education ministry.

Authorities were also on alert in Barcelona after an anonymous TikTok network called Blocus urged new gatherings, and in Italy following recent clashes in Milan, Turin and Bologna.

Practical implications and verification

The interior ministry had deployed 70,000 police and gendarmes, including elite units, ahead of Saturday’s demonstrations. Nuñez warned that the day looked like “a very high risk” for violence and said officers were prepared for confrontation.

Readers can verify the original announcement through the French interior ministry’s official communications and the Paris police prefecture’s public statements. Details on arrest totals, injury counts and deployment figures come from those official sources, while protester quotes and descriptions of specific clashes reflect reporting from the scene rather than independent verification by this article.

Unknowns include the full extent of property damage outside Frankfurt, whether the announced Tuesday and Thursday student blockades took place, and the outcome of the planned 5 November demonstration.
